name: Maya Yoshida
status: Free agent. His LA Galaxy contract ended on 20 Nov 2026. He has NOT announced retirement. Next step: undecided.
summary: Japanese centre-back (a defender who plays in the middle of the back line). He played in the top division of six countries, captained Japan at a World Cup, and captained LA Galaxy to the 2024 MLS Cup.
quick_facts: 2007 to 2026: Japan, Netherlands, England, Italy, Germany, USA
580 matches, 36 goals (all competitions, added up from the season table below)
Waseda University, School of Human Sciences (correspondence course), graduated 2019
President of the Japan Pro-Footballers Association (players' union) since 2022
seasons_note: Matches in all competitions (league, cups, continental). Source: English Wikipedia career table for 2007 to 2025; LA Galaxy official totals (117 matches, 8 goals) for the club total; 2026 is from Soccer King (28 matches, 2 goals), which matches the club total. Other sites count 2026 differently (see 'Not verified').

timeline.event: Born in Nagasaki, the youngest of three brothers.
Passes the Nagoya Grampus youth trial on a family trip, expecting to fail. Leaves home and moves to Aichi with an older brother.
Chooses a public high school (Toyota High School) partly to study English seriously, already aiming to play abroad.
Turns professional with Nagoya Grampus. Starts a Waseda University correspondence degree.
Plays at the Beijing Olympics (U-23). Wins a regular centre-back place at Nagoya under coach Dragan Stojković.
Best season in Japan: 48 matches, 8 goals. Signs for VVV-Venlo in December.
Senior Japan debut (6 Jan). Breaks a foot bone days after arriving in the Netherlands and misses about 10 months. Dutch league debut on 30 Oct.
Wins the AFC Asian Cup with Japan (first Japan goal, also a red card in the quarter-final). Scores against PSV in September.
Captains Japan to 4th place at the London Olympics. Joins Southampton (Premier League) for about £3 million on 30 Aug. Announces his marriage.
First full Premier League season: 34 matches. Criticised in Japan after the Confederations Cup.
First World Cup (Brazil): starts all 3 matches. At Southampton he is back-up behind Lovren and Fonte.
New 3-year Southampton contract (Jan). A back-pass mistake against Manchester United (Sept) sends him back to the bench.
Still third-choice at Southampton; uses cup games to stay ready. First child (a daughter) born.

Breakthrough year: captains Southampton for the first time (18 Jan), plays the League Cup final at Wembley (26 Feb), first match as Japan captain (23 Mar), first Japanese player to reach 100 Premier League matches (29 Apr), new contract to 2020.
World Cup in Russia: plays every minute; Japan lose 3–2 to Belgium after leading 2–0. Becomes permanent Japan captain after Makoto Hasebe. Publishes his book 'Unbeatable Mind'.

Asian Cup runner-up as captain (his handball gives away a penalty in the final). Gets UK permanent residency. Graduates from Waseda. Pledges 1% of his wages to the Saints Foundation charity. 100th cap for Japan (14 Nov).
Moves to Sampdoria (Italy) on loan on deadline day (31 Jan). Debuts 8 Mar, right before lockdown. Donates 10,000 masks in Genoa. Gives a club interview in Italian by August.
Captains Japan to 4th at the Tokyo Olympics (his third Games). Scores against Inter Milan (12 Sept). Becomes Japan's most-capped centre-back (Nov).
Becomes president of the players' union (20 June). Joins Schalke 04 (5 July). Captains Japan at the Qatar World Cup: wins over Germany and Spain; loses to Croatia on penalties (his kick is saved).
Schalke are relegated (dropped to the second division). Joins LA Galaxy on 3 Aug. Left out of the Japan squad as a new generation takes over.
Captain of LA Galaxy. Starts every league match. Wins the MLS Cup (7 Dec), his first club trophy. Club Defender of the Year.
Signs a new 2-year deal (18 Jan) with a pay cut. Galaxy have a very bad season (14th in the West).

Farewell match for Japan (31 May, 127th cap). Travels to the World Cup as a non-playing support member. Gets a US green card (16 July). Loses his starting place from September; knee injury. Contract ends 20 Nov; future undecided.

achievements.item: MLS Cup winner (as captain), LA Galaxy
Three World Cups (11 matches); captain in 2022; round of 16 in 2018 and 2022
Three Olympics; captain twice; 4th place twice
127 caps for Japan: most ever by a Japanese centre-back; reported as 3rd on Japan's all-time list
First Japanese player to reach 100 Premier League matches; 154 in total is still the most by a Japanese player
Captain of Southampton (matches), Japan, Japan Olympic team, and LA Galaxy; vice-captain at Schalke
LA Galaxy Defender of the Year (a club award)
University degree from Waseda while playing in the Premier League (took about 12 years)
President of the Japan Pro-Footballers Association; started the player-voted JPFA Awards

leadership_intro: Short answer: he was almost never the most talented player in the room. He earned trust the slow way, and he did the same things again in every new country. Eight patterns show up again and again.

leadership.title: He planned for language years before he needed it
leadership.simple: He decided as a teenager that he wanted to play in Europe, then worked backward: 'So I must learn English now.' In each new country he learned the local language fast and used it in public, even when it was not perfect.
evidence: Chose a public high school partly so he could study English properly, already aiming abroad.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/sk_column/article/84825.html
Took English conversation lessons before leaving Japan; giving interviews in English by 2011.
https://gendai.media/articles/-/22834
Japan captain Hasebe handed him the job of talking to referees in English when he took over the armband (2017).
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/828172
Italy: used Genoa's local dialect in his debut-day interview, and it went viral. Six months later he did a club interview in Italian.
https://telenord.it/sampdoria-il-genovese-di-yoshida-e-virale-sul-web-cianin-cianin

leadership.title: He speaks up early instead of staying quiet
leadership.simple: Many foreign players stay silent until they feel safe. He does the opposite. He says what the team needs to hear, even as the new person.
evidence: Italy, 4 months in: shouted 'Parlate!' (Talk!) at a silent defence.
https://www.clubdoria46.it/sampdoria-parlate-urla-yoshida-la-difesa-e-muta/
Germany, 3 weeks in: said on TV that Schalke's squad was too big and had to improve.
https://www.watson.de/sport/fussball/640887259-schalke-04-maya-yoshida-mit-deutlichen-worten-zu-schalke-04-und-klassenerhalt
After the 2018 World Cup loss to Belgium he said Japan had been naive and fragile, and asked for a rethink of youth development.
https://inside.fifa.com/news/yoshida-japan-must-think-seriously-about-the-future
2021: publicly asked for the no-spectator decision at the Tokyo Olympics to be reconsidered.
https://www.footballchannel.jp/2021/07/18/post429576/

leadership.title: He takes the blame first, then explains
leadership.simple: When things go wrong he names his own mistake before anything else. This is a big reason people keep trusting him after bad days.
evidence: 2019 Asian Cup final: blamed himself for not removing the team's complacency.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/news/japan/national/20190204/902335.html
Schalke 2022: said his own performance was not good enough; he won his place back and the coach publicly asked for a new contract for him by March 2023.
https://www.goal.com/jp/%E3%83%8B%E3%83%A5%E3%83%BC%E3%82%B9/Bundesliga-Schalke-Maya-Yoshida-20230303/blt2161e75a2e5216e4
In 2024 he still said the Schalke relegation was his responsibility as a captain figure.
https://sportiva.shueisha.co.jp/clm/football/wfootball/2024/07/09/post_84/
2015: admitted his back-pass error against Manchester United to reporters straight after.
https://sportiva.shueisha.co.jp/clm/football/wfootball/2015/09/23/post_852/

leadership.title: He waits on the bench without complaining, then takes his chance
leadership.simple: At Southampton he was back-up for years under several managers. He did not complain in public. He fixed his weak points and was ready when the chance came.
evidence: Third-choice for long spells, then captain within months in 2017. Teammate Shinji Okazaki credited his patience.
https://news.livedoor.com/article/detail/12586536/
Manager Ronald Koeman praised his attitude and said he puts the team before himself (2015).
https://www.skysports.com/football/news/11700/9629102/southampton-defender-maya-yoshida-signs-a-new-three-year-contract
A review of his book notes he rarely criticises the managers who dropped him.
https://wsc.co.uk/?p=8248
LA Galaxy: said he first had to play well to earn trust; then started every league match of the 2024 title season at age 36.
https://www.lagalaxy.com/news/la-galaxy-announce-2024-team-awards

leadership.title: Humour and 'younger-brother power' make him easy to approach
leadership.simple: He is the youngest of three brothers and grew up in a house full of guests. He learned to get along with older people and to make people laugh. He calls this 'younger-brother power' (弟力).
evidence: Former J.League chairman Mitsuru Murai says Yoshida names 'younger-brother power' as his greatest strength.
https://president.jp/articles/-/64502?page=2
After his first Premier League match as captain he joked that the best part was not stumbling over the team talk.
https://www.footballchannel.jp/?p=206051
VVV-Venlo chairman Hai Berden remembers a cheerful, serious and responsible newcomer.
https://number.bunshun.jp/articles/-/813744

leadership.title: He gives back to the town he lives in
leadership.simple: He treats each city as home, not as a stop. Local people notice this, and it builds trust outside the dressing room too.
evidence: Southampton 2019: pledged 1% of his wages to the club's charity, to thank the city and set an example for young players.
https://www.premierleague.com/news/1312017
Genoa 2020: bought 10,000 masks for hospitals and club staff after playing only one match there.
https://www.sampdoria.it/en/news-en-2/team-en-2/2020/05/29/yoshida-donates-10000-protective-masks-to-genoa-hospitals-and-samp-employees/
Nagasaki: posts every 9 August (atomic bomb anniversary), in Japanese and English.
https://www.soccerdigestweb.com/news/detail/id=114846

leadership.title: He holds the door open for the next players
leadership.simple: He helps younger players, even the ones competing for his own position, and he guides Japanese players who move abroad after him.
evidence: Coached young defender Jack Stephens through his early matches; Stephens later named him the ex-teammate he would most want back.
https://sportsbeatfeed.co.uk/?p=11531
Takumi Minamino phoned him for advice before joining Southampton on loan (2021).
https://www.southamptonfc.com/en/news/article/minamino-reveals-yoshidas-influence
Yukinari Sugawara called him a legend; Yoshida texted him about the move and joked he could live in his house (2024).
https://www.southamptonfc.com/en/news/article/sugawara-inspired-by-legend-yoshida
Ran casual English lessons for younger Japan teammates at team meals.
https://president.jp/articles/-/64502

leadership.title: He leads even when he is not playing, and he builds systems
leadership.simple: Late in his career he showed that leadership is not only wearing the armband. He served the team from outside the squad, and he changed rules for all players through the union.
evidence: 2026 World Cup: gave up a TV job to travel as a non-playing support member, linking players and coaches.
https://www.lagalaxy.com/news/maya-yoshida-finds-a-new-way-to-lead-through-2026-world-cup-experience
Coach Hajime Moriyasu thanked him for unifying the players and for constant communication over the years.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/news/japan/national/20260530/2165095.html
Union president: J.League minimum salaries and the end of the old A/B/C contract system (decided 2024, from 2026).
https://daily.co.jp/soccer/2024/09/24/0018156230.shtml
Created the player-voted JPFA Awards (first ceremony Jan 2023), modelled on England's PFA awards.
https://www.soccer-king.jp/news/japan/japan_other/20230118/1730848.html

honest_view: He was not a flawless player. Famous mistakes: the 2015 back-pass against Manchester United, the handball in the 2019 Asian Cup final, and a saved penalty against Croatia in 2022.
Schalke was a failure on the pitch: the team was relegated and German media criticised him strongly.
He has only two major trophies (Asian Cup 2011 and MLS Cup 2024). His reputation is built on long service and leadership more than on winning.

'No other centre-back played in so many countries' is hard to prove. The safe statement: he played in the top division of six countries, which is very rare for any defender. I did not check every other player to prove he is the only one.
The claim that he was the 'first Japanese captain in the Premier League' is likely true but I could not find a source that proves it as a first.

roots.title: A house full of people
roots.text: His father liked a lively home and later opened a boarding house. Guests were always around, so Maya grew up talking with older people. He connects his easy way with people to this.

roots.title: Youngest of three brothers
roots.text: His eldest brother Honami, about seven years older and a goalkeeper, trained him hard and taught him to keep his head up. He practised on the steep slope outside the house.

roots.title: First club: Nanryo FC (南陵FC)
roots.text: He began at a local primary-school team in Nagasaki. He was a striker then. He started watching videos of his own matches at home as a child.

roots.title: Left home at 12
roots.text: He took the Nagoya Grampus youth trial 'as a souvenir' on a family trip and passed. A brother moved to Aichi to live with him. He was homesick, and seeing how much the move cost his family made him decide he had to become a professional.

roots.title: School and study
roots.text: He picked a public high school over the club-linked one so he would not get special treatment and could study English. He often studied through the night in exam periods. Later he finished a Waseda University degree by correspondence in 2019.

roots.title: From striker to centre-back
roots.text: His position moved backward as he grew: striker, then midfielder, then centre-back as a professional. Early mentors included Nagoya's Yutaka Akita, youth coach Park Jae-hyun, and first-team coaches Sef Vergoossen and Dragan Stojković.

roots.title: Nagasaki and peace
roots.text: He wrote a poem about war in second grade. As an adult he posts every 9 August about the atomic bombing, in two languages, and trains with hometown club V-Varen Nagasaki in the off-season.

roots.title: A promise to his father
roots.text: His father told his sons to dream big and not become 'football fools'. Number magazine reported that the 2024 MLS title fulfilled a promise to his late father.

notes: No amounts are public for any sponsor deal, book, or media job.
No reliable report was found of a company he owns, an investment, or a football school.
No trustworthy source publishes his total career earnings or net worth. Websites that do are guessing.
'Guaranteed compensation' in MLS means base salary plus guaranteed bonuses, averaged per year. It is not exactly the cash paid in that year.
The 2023 to 2025 MLS numbers were seen through Spotrac and news reports, not read from the union's own files. The 2026 number was read directly.

unverified: Catholic faith and a rosary from the Vatican: found only on English Wikipedia. Not treated as fact here.
'I feel 25 percent English': the Japanese report of that interview has him joking that he understands about 25% of English. Exact wording unconfirmed.
Baseball pitcher Tsuyoshi Shimoyanagi as his 'uncle': Japanese Wikipedia describes a more distant relative.
Who the boarding house is for: one report says high-school students from remote islands; not confirmed directly.
Meaning of the name 'Maya': three different versions exist; he says his parents tell it differently each time.
Eredivisie Goal of the Season 2011–12: only English Wikipedia states the award.
Details of his 2010 foot injury differ between sources (all agree on about 10 months out).
'First Japanese to captain a Premier League team': likely, but no source proves it as a first.
2026 match count: Soccer King says 28 (used here); Rotowire says 23 league matches; Wikipedia is out of date.
LA Galaxy say '722 career appearances'; my season-by-season club total is 580 plus 127 Japan caps. The club may count differently.
All-time Japan caps rank (3rd): reported by Soccer King; the full list was not checked line by line.
Whether he is still union president after mid-2026: last confirmed in November 2025.
GM Will Kuntz's 20 Nov 2026 comments were read through Japanese reports, so wording is a translation.
Rumours linking him with V-Varen Nagasaki or Nagoya are fan talk and one tabloid report. Nothing official.
Direct YouTube links were not confirmed; the appendix uses YouTube search links by exact title.
A YouTube channel exists under his name, but I could not confirm it is official, so it is not linked.
